name: either
intent: Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention.
problem: An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.
context: Expected, recoverable failures in code that has to compose: parsing and validation at a boundary, persistence and I/O calls, service calls inside a pipeline, or any layer whose caller must render, translate, retry or count the failure. It pays off where the error type is part of an API contract between teams or modules, and where the language can express a two-case type (algebraic data type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union) or a library supplies one.
benefits: The outcome is in the type: a caller cannot consume the result without destructuring it, so an unhandled failure is a visible decision - or, with exhaustiveness checking, a compile error - instead of a missing catch block.
The reason travels with the failure as a domain value, so callers branch on concrete cases (errors.Is/errors.As, a sealed variant, an exception class kept as data) rather than parsing message text.
Fallible steps compose: map/flatMap/and_then/? chains a sequence of operations and short-circuits at the first failure while preserving its reason, instead of nesting conditionals or try blocks.
Boundary conversion becomes explicit: exceptions, status codes and nullable returns are translated into one place, which is exactly where logging, translation and retry policy belong.
Both branches are ordinary values, so tests construct them directly - nothing has to be thrown, caught or mocked to exercise the failure path.

Failure as data can be serialized, queued, counted and aggregated (error budgets, validation reports), and independent failures can be accumulated instead of fail-fast where the caller needs every reason.
tradeoffs: Signature noise: Either<Error, T> spreads through the call chain, and the error type becomes part of the API contract, so changing the reason type ripples through every function that propagates it.
Verbosity at call sites in languages without ? or for-comprehension sugar: each step needs a branch or a chained combinator, and the happy path loses its directness.
Lost context: an exception captures a throw site, a cause chain and a stack automatically; a returned value carries only what the reason type stores, so diagnostic depth has to be designed in.
Two error channels coexist: stdlib and third-party code still throw, so the conversion at the boundary is manual and easy to omit, leaving callers to handle both.
Escape hatches reintroduce the crash: unwrap/get/value!/expect on a failure branch is an exception in disguise, and teams need a convention that keeps it in tests and documented invariants.
Per-result allocation in Java, JavaScript and Python is measurable in hot loops; the allocation-free realizations (Rust, C++, Swift) are not available in every language.
Nesting (Either<E, Either<E, T>>, Result<Result<...>>) appears as soon as composition uses map instead of flatMap, and generic error unions grow unwieldy without union types or row polymorphism.

participants.responsibility: Holds exactly one of the two branches at a time; the tag/disjoint union makes the payload that is not active unreachable.
Carries the value the operation produced when it succeeded.
Carries the reason the operation failed - the branch that makes the pattern different from Option/Maybe.
Domain value describing the failure (enum, sealed variant, record, custom error type); it must hold enough data for the caller to branch and to render, and must not be a formatted message string.
Returns Either instead of throwing or signalling through a sentinel; converts exceptions to values at the boundary where the local error semantics are known.
Consumes the value by taking one handler per branch, so both branches are handled exactly once and nowhere else.

use_cases: Validating untrusted input at a boundary and returning the concrete reason (field, offset, rule violated) so the caller can render a precise message.
Domain operations that can fail for several business reasons (insufficient funds, account closed, limit exceeded) where callers must branch on the reason instead of guessing from a string.
Parsing and decoding (config, documents, wire formats) where the failure position or cause must travel back with the outcome.
Pipelines of fallible steps (authenticate -> load -> transform -> persist) that should stop at the first failure with the original reason intact instead of unwinding with a stack trace.
Translate-once boundaries: turn transport errors into domain errors in one adapter, so no layer above has to know about HTTP codes, IOExceptions or database error numbers.

Accumulating validation of independent fields, where every reason must be reported together rather than only the first one — use an Applicative validation instance with a Semigroup-based error accumulator.
Callbacks and async APIs whose failure cannot be thrown to the caller (completion handlers, event consumers) and therefore has to be delivered as a value.
Parallel fallible operations where you want to collect all successes and all failures separately before deciding, using partition or sequence operations on a List<Result>.
Domain-driven design aggregates where a root entity operation can fail for many reasons (invariant violations, business rule breaches) and the aggregate root returns Either to the application layer.
Service-to-service calls inside a pipeline where the downstream service returns a structured error response (not an exception), and the upstream must branch, translate, or propagate it.

Rust standard-library convention: fallible I/O, parsing and system calls return Result<T, E> and ? propagates the first Err up the call chain to a boundary (a main or entry point that returns Result) - the backbone of recoverable error handling in Rust.
Kotlin/Arrow typed-error pipelines: an either { } computation DSL where bind() short-circuits on Left and Either.catch turns a throwing interop call into a Left at the adapter boundary.
Java services using Vavr's right-biased Either: map/flatMap chains propagate Left without checked exceptions, keeping the failure type part of the signature in fluent pipelines.
avoid_when: The failure is genuinely exceptional - a broken invariant, a programming error, an out-of-memory condition: throw or panic; an Either adds ceremony with no caller that can act on it.
The caller only needs to know whether it worked and no reason matters: use Option/Maybe, a bool, or an empty Result instead.

The language's dominant idiom is exceptions and it cannot force the caller to look at a returned value (plain Ruby, older Java, dynamic Python): a well-designed exception hierarchy has less friction than a value branch nobody checks.
The operation is already total - it returns a value for every input - so there is no second outcome to encode.
Failure is so frequent and the call volume so high that a wrapper allocation dominates the hot loop: a status code or the language-native result type is cheaper.
There is exactly one call site inside one function: a plain early return or an if/else is simpler than introducing a type and its combinators.
The two outcomes are not success-versus-failure but two equally legitimate results: use a general sum type / variant, not an error-shaped Either.
anti_patterns: Either<String, T> everywhere: stringly-typed reasons force callers back to parsing messages, and the reason that mattered is lost in formatting.
Immediate unwrapping at the boundary (unwrap(), get(), value!, getOrThrow) so the failure crashes exactly where an exception would have — an Either-shaped exception.
Using Either as general control flow: loop breaks, three-way results and 'no value' all encoded as Left, turning a two-outcome contract into an untyped variant.
Mixed contracts in one API (throw for some failures, Left for others) so that callers have to write both rescue and branch handling, and always forget one.
Nesting Either<E, Either<E, T>> (or Result<Result<...>>) instead of flattening with flatMap, which produces type names nobody can read.
Serializing the wrapper as-is ({"Left": {...}} on the wire), which leaks the implementation type into the protocol and forces clients to know the language's representation.
Using map where flatMap/bind is needed, producing a nested Either<E, Either<E, T>> that then requires a second flatten — the caller should not have to undo accidental nesting.
Designing a single flat string error type that is used both for machine-readable branching and human-readable messages, when the two concerns (code and text) need different representations.
Applying ROP/flatMap chaining to operations that are not genuinely compositional — introducing the Either machinery for a single call site where a plain early return or if/else is simpler.
Using Either for symmetric alternatives (Left/Right both carry meaningful business outcomes) — the two-case form should signal failure vs success, not merely two equally valid results.
design_principles: Make failure visible: encode expected failures in the signature (a total function over outcomes) instead of in hidden control flow.
Single responsibility: the value carries the outcome, the caller owns the policy (render, retry, translate, default).
Information hiding and typing: callers branch on domain cases, never on message text.
Composition over special syntax: map/flatMap make the fallible computation a first-class value that composes like any other.
Explicit contracts: the reason type is part of the signature, so a change in the failure contract is a visible, compile-checked change rather than a surprise at runtime.
best_practices: Make the reason a domain type (enum, sealed variant, record, custom error) carrying the data the caller needs; keep human-readable messages for rendering only — never for branching.
Convert exceptions to values exactly once, at the boundary that owns the semantics, and keep the exception itself as the reason when its type says everything there is to say.
Flatten with flatMap/and_then/bind — never build nested Either<Either> or Result<Result> by mapping a function that already returns one; use flatten when the inner wrapper leaks through.
Keep the success path monadic and the failure path plain (return the failure early) so the happy path stays readable; resist branching inside the happy path.

Reserve unwrap/expect/getOrThrow accessors for tests and documented invariants; provide orElse/recover/getOrElse/map_err as the production exits — and document which errors can legitimately trigger each path.
Add conversions you need once (toOption, mapLeft, sequence, traverse) instead of branching ad hoc at every call site; centralize them in a shared module.
Serialize the reason through an explicit wire schema; never let the language's Either representation become the protocol — translate at the boundary to a documented error code or message object.

Document the convention (Left/Err is the failure) and enforce it in one place: the constructors and helpers everybody imports; a shared Result type alias or a module-level convention beats an ad-hoc convention.

Use right-bias consistently: map and flatMap always operate on the Right/Ok/Success branch; Left/Err/Failure propagates unchanged through every combinator — this is what makes for-comprehensions work.

In validation scenarios where you need every error, not just the first, use an Applicative instance with a Semigroup that concatenates errors (fp-ts getApplicativeValidation, Scala's validation, or a manual combine with a Left-list).

Use map vs bind correctly: map transforms the success value only when it is already Ok; bind (flatMap/and_then) chains a function that itself returns Either — using map where bind is needed produces nested Either, and using bind where map suffices is verbose.
Design error types as a sealed hierarchy that mirrors the domain's failure modes; a flat string enum is acceptable only when the error space is truly one-dimensional and will never grow.

At service boundaries, translate once and only once: external errors (HTTP status, DB exception codes, network failures) become domain errors in the adapter layer, so no layer above has to know about them.
Avoid the 'Either<String, T>' antipattern: a string error forces callers back to parsing message text, defeats exhaustiveness checking, and loses type-level information about what went wrong.

Prefer railway-oriented composition (pipe/chain) over nested if/else or try/catch blocks; the ? operator in Rust, and_then in fp-ts, and bind in returns-Python all express the same intent — short-circuit on failure, pass success forward.
sources: Haskell base library, Data.Either - the canonical Left/Right two-constructor datatype of the functional tradition, with its Functor/Monad instances (https://hackage.haskell.org/package/base/docs/Data-Either.html).
Wikipedia, Tagged union - the ML/Haskell origin of compiler-checked sum types and the tag that makes the two cases safe to discriminate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagged_union).

Scala standard library scaladoc, scala.util.Either - a value of one of two possible types (a disjoint union); Left failure / Right success convention, right-biased map and flatMap, for-comprehension limits (https://www.scala-lang.org/api/current/scala/util/Either.html).

cppreference, std::expected (C++23) - the C++ realisation, including the note that Rust's Result and Haskell's Either provide the same functionality; monadic .and_then, .or_else, .transform, .transform_error methods (https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/expected).

fp-ts Either documentation - the TypeScript realisation with the same Left/Right convention, match/fold, right-bias, and validation variants that accumulate errors via getApplicativeValidation with a Semigroup (https://gcanti.github.io/fp-ts/modules/Either.ts.html).

returns (Python) Result/Success/Failure documentation - the Python realisation with bind/map composition, @safe decorator for exception-to-Result conversion, pipeline.do notation, and structural pattern matching integration (https://returns.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/result.html).

Rust std::result documentation - the canonical Result<Ok, Err> enum with exhaustive combinators: map, map_err, and_then, or_else, unwrap, expect, ? operator; guidelines on when to panic vs return Result (https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/result/enum.Result.html).

Scott Wlaschin, Railway Oriented Programming - a functional error-handling recipe using the two-track (Success/Failure) model; bind, map, switch, tee, tryCatch, doubleMap, plus combinators; the bind/flatMap adapter that converts a switch function to two-track input; Kleisli composition >=>; parallel validation with &&& (https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/rop/).

Scott Wlaschin, Against Railway-Oriented Programming - a cautionary note on overusing ROP; warnings about complexity creep, when plain exceptions or early returns are simpler, and when the two-track model is overkill (https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/posts/against-railway-oriented-programming/).

fp-ts core Either module - getAltValidation/getApplicativeValidation for accumulating all errors (not just first) using a Semigroup; tapError for logging without consuming; firstRightOf for picking first success; orElseEither for chaining with widened types (https://fp-ts.github.io/core/modules/Either.ts.html).

Arrow Kotlin documentation, Either & Ior & Result - the Kotlin realisation: the either { } computation DSL with bind()/raise(), Either.catch converting exceptions to Left, and error accumulation with zipOrAccumulate (https://arrow-kt.io/learn/typed-errors/wrappers/either-and-ior/).

Vavr user guide, Either - the Java realisation: a right-biased functional container with map, flatMap and filterOrElse so Java pipelines propagate Left without checked exceptions (https://docs.vavr.io/).

The Rust Programming Language, chapter 9.2, Recoverable Errors with Result - Ok/Err as the language-standard channel for expected failures, unwrap/expect as deliberate panic hatches, and guidance on when to return Result instead of panicking (https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html).

Leandro Ostera, Exceptions are Ok - a critique of blanket Result/Either use: the wrapper hides which calls can raise and forces per-layer map_error boilerplate and wrapper error types, while untracked exceptions propagate for free (https://leostera.substack.com/p/exceptions-are-ok).

Oskar Dudycz, Throw, Result, or neither? - an argument that a Result wrapper rarely changes persistence, retry or continuation decisions, that a throw after a recorded event cannot undo it, and that the choice depends on the workflow rather than the type (https://www.architecture-weekly.com/p/throw-result-or-neither).
